# Beyond agreement: a benchmark of how language models grade student work, and how they fail

# Language models that agree with expert raters can still be moved by a note in the answer, give way when a student objects, and write feedback that follows a grade they are told

David S. Porcaro, Learning Design Alliance

Research and writing carried out with Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic). See AI use.

# Abstract

Language models are being used to grade student work and to write feedback on it, and the evidence offered for them is usually their agreement with human raters on a public dataset. This paper asks how closely 22 prompted language models agree with expert raters on short answers, programs and essays, measured against the raters' agreement with each other and against scorers trained on graded answers, and how each model fails when the work, the context or the conversation is altered in a way whose correct response is known in advance. Every model graded the same 100 items per task through one plain prompt, under zero data retention for every model but one (Claude Fable 5.1, run only on public corpora under its maker's 30-day retention), then altered versions of them, and every probe and every study verdict, except six named sets of statistics, was first checked on simulated graders with a planted effect. On short answers 18 of the 22 models have point estimates above the raters' agreement with each other, but for none does the whole interval lie above it; on code four models are shown to agree with the raters more than the raters agree with each other; and on essays no point estimate reaches the raters' published agreement and 18 of the 22 are shown to fall below it, while a fine-tuned scorer (QWK 0.809Printed0.809Source value0.808694Filecode/out/baselines.jsonFieldrows › {'model': 'baseline: deberta-ft', 'task': 'asap2'} › qwk › estimateAnalysisstandard-checks (release file)Build checkmatches at build) has a higher point estimate than every model. Agreement with raters on ordinary work is therefore not sufficient evidence that a model grades the work it is given, and the evaluation of a grader needs to test how it fails as well as how often it agrees.

# 1. Introduction

Language models are now asked to grade student work and to write the feedback that comes with a grade. A model can grade an essay, a program or a short answer in seconds, and it can explain its grade in words. The case for adopting such a grader usually rests on one number: its agreement with human raters on a public dataset, often reported as quadratic weighted kappa (QWK). Agreement is one of the checks that testing organizations apply before trusting a machine's scores (Williamson, Xi and Breyer 2012), but the same framework treats it as one piece of evidence among several, and studies of automated scoring have long shown why.

The reason is that a grader can agree with raters on ordinary work and still not grade the work it is given. Before language models, expert writers who knew how a scoring engine worked could raise its scores without writing better essays (Powers et al. 2002), gibberish and shuffled answers were often given credit by content-scoring systems (Ding et al. 2020), and a fixed string added to a short answer could earn a passing grade (Filighera, Steuer and Rensing 2020). Language models add new ways to fail. Instructions placed inside the data a model processes can override its own instructions (Greshake et al. 2023), and a student's answer is exactly such data: notes asking a language-model grader for full credit often succeed (Li et al. 2026), and short phrases appended to a text inflate the scores of language models used as judges (Raina, Liusie and Gales 2024). A grader that a student can talk to can also be persuaded to change its grade, and one that writes feedback can write feedback that follows the grade it is given rather than the work. None of these failures is visible in an agreement figure computed on ordinary answers.

Agreement itself is harder to read than it looks. Two expert raters do not agree perfectly, so a model's QWK means little without the raters' agreement with each other beside it, and corpora differ widely in how well their raters agree. Scorers trained on thousands of a corpus's own graded essays already exceed the raters' published agreement on ASAP 2.0 (Ormerod and Kehat 2025), but a new question comes with no graded answers to train on, and a trained scorer gives a grade without feedback. The evidence a school or a vendor needs is therefore broader than one agreement figure: how a grader compares with the human reference and with trained scorers, how it responds to work designed to move it, whether it holds its grade and writes feedback about the work, whether it grades recordings as well as text, whether it treats groups of students alike, and what it costs to run.

This paper reports a benchmark built to provide that evidence for prompted language models. A fixed battery of public student work, each item with grades from expert human raters, is graded by every model through the same plain prompt, together with altered versions of the same work, called probes, whose correct response is known in advance: a blank answer should receive the lowest grade, and a request for full marks appended to an answer should not raise it. This is the invariance and directional testing of behavioral evaluation in natural language processing (Ribeiro et al. 2020), which robustness studies of essay scorers have used to argue that agreement alone is not enough (Kabra et al. 2022; Wang, Hu and Zhao 2024); the benchmark applies it across many models, tasks and media and to the conversation and the feedback around a grade. Agreement is reported as a share of the raters' own agreement and beside scorers trained on the same corpus. Every probe and every study verdict, except six sets of statistics named in Section 4.6, was first run on simulated graders built to resemble the real ones, with an effect planted and without one, a simulation study of each statistic in the sense of Morris, White and Crowther (2019); a measure whose check did not find the planted effect is reported as unmeasured. The benchmark covers 22 language models on short answers, programs and essays, models that grade speech, handwritten work and video, the fairness of grades across groups of students, and the energy, carbon and water a grading uses. Section 2 reviews the literature for each of the six research questions in Section 3, Section 4 describes the method, Section 5 reports the results, and Sections 6 to 8 discuss them, set out the threats to their validity and conclude.

# 2. Background

# 2.1 Agreement with expert raters

The standard framework for evaluating automated scoring asks for agreement between machine and human scores alongside evidence about what the scores measure (Williamson, Xi and Breyer 2012). Agreement is usually reported as QWK, which is sensitive to the rating scale, to how scores are distributed and to sample size, so comparing it across tasks with different scales, or on small samples, can mislead (Doewes, Kurdhi and Saxena 2023; Albatarni and Elsayed 2026). A human reference is needed beside it. On the Mohler short-answer corpus, two graders working with no instructions beyond the scale gave the same grade 57.7% of the time, and one was systematically more generous (Mohler, Bunescu and Mihalcea 2011). Calderon, Reichart and Dror (2025) proposed a statistical test of whether a language model can replace a human annotator against such a reference, and large studies of language models as judges find that agreement varies widely across models, datasets and the property judged (Bavaresco et al. 2025).

For short answers, a combined benchmark that includes the Mohler corpus found prompted GPT-4o still well short of human performance, although its human reference was borrowed from another corpus (Meyer, Breuer and Fürst 2024). Studies of prompted models against trained scorers mostly find the trained scorers ahead on short answers (Kortemeyer 2023; Chamieh, Zesch and Giebermann 2024; Ferreira Mello et al. 2025). On essays the consensus is the same. On ASAP 2.0, the essay corpus used here, fine-tuned models already exceed the raters' published agreement of κ 0.745 (Ormerod and Kehat 2025), and prompted models scoring the same corpus and two others reach a QWK of about 0.6 with a stable harsh bias on grammar and conventions (Kucia, Chakraborty and Wróblewska 2026). The direction in which prompted models depart from the raters differs between studies: on the original ASAP corpus they graded lower than the raters (Kundu and Barbosa 2024), and on German secondary essays higher (Seßler et al. 2025). Essay length predicts essay grades, so an essay scorer's agreement has long been set against what length alone predicts (Chodorow and Burstein 2004); a recent study of small open models reports a length-only QWK beside the raters' ceiling and finds the models below both (Nguyen et al. 2026). For programs, a comparison of 18 models from four vendors on more than 6,000 introductory submissions found systematic differences in strictness between and within vendors (Jukiewicz 2026), without a second human grade to set them against.

# 2.2 Moving the grade without improving the work

Attempts to move a machine grade predate language models. Expert writers raised a scoring engine's grades more easily than they lowered them (Powers et al. 2002), universal trigger phrases let short answers pass without answering the question (Filighera, Steuer and Rensing 2020), and gibberish or shuffled answers were often credited (Ding et al. 2020). For language-model graders the nearest prior study tested role play, iterative and many-shot attacks on five models across short answers and essays, found a mean attack success of 56.9%, and found that an instruction to ignore such notes lowered success without removing it (Li et al. 2026). Optimized attacks compromise short-answer grading agents further (Li, Zhou, Liu and Wu 2026). In a test of nine models, directives hidden in code submissions misled the grader, with failure above 95% for some large open models (Sahoo et al. 2026), persuasive phrasing embedded in otherwise identical solutions inflated judges' scores and survived counter-prompting (Hwang et al. 2025), and injection risk has been assessed in grading a national essay exam (Karjus et al. 2026). Outside student grading, short universal phrases appended to a text inflate the scores of language models used as judges (Raina, Liusie and Gales 2024). A constant response unrelated to the input can even top automatic benchmarks judged by language models (Zheng et al. 2025). The general mechanism is indirect prompt injection: instructions placed in the data a model processes can override its developer's instructions (Greshake et al. 2023).

Defenses are mixed. Training a model to rank its developer's instructions above those in its input greatly increases robustness (Wallace et al. 2024), and marking untrusted input with delimiters or encodings cut attack success to below 2% in one study (Hines et al. 2024), but no model separates instructions from data reliably (Zverev et al. 2025), and across 13 judges no single defense dominated (Li, Xu, et al. 2025). More reasoning at inference time improved robustness for two reasoning models across many attacks (Zaremba et al. 2025), unless the adversary can see the reasoning (Wu et al. 2025). The wording of a prompt matters as well: results from a single prompt are brittle across 20 language models (Mizrahi et al. 2024), meaning-preserving format changes move accuracy by up to 76 points (Sclar et al. 2024), and for language-model judges, rewording the prompt lowered agreement on all four tasks of a benchmark that sets each judge's result beside its agreement with itself on the same prompt (Bellibatlu, Raff and Zhang 2026). A model served at reduced numerical precision kept its trustworthiness at 4-bit in one study (Hong et al. 2024), but providers may serve models that differ from the reference weights (Gao, Liang and Guestrin 2025). Human graders are biased by irrelevant information about a student, including poor prior performance (Malouff and Thorsteinsson 2016), and language models encode differing expectations of competence from students' names (Sakunkoo and Sakunkoo 2025). An achievement attribute in the prompt changes how language models judge identical essays in their feedback (Tan, Phalen and Demszky 2026), and an attainment label moved a language-model short-answer grader's grade on identical work on six models (Porcaro 2026).

# 2.3 Pushback, the working and feedback

Language models tend to agree with the person they are talking to. Larger models repeat back a user's preferred answer (Perez et al. 2022), assistants trained on human preferences are consistently sycophantic (Sharma et al. 2023), and asking "Are you sure?" made ten models change their answer 46% of the time on average (Laban et al. 2023). Models endorse a counterargument more when it arrives as a casual follow-up turn than when it is set out beside the original position (Kim and Khashabi 2025), and in an educational setting a student mentioning a wrong answer lowered model correctness by up to 15 percentage points (Arvin 2025). Sycophancy can move a model toward a correct answer as well as away from it, and the two have been reported separately (Fanous et al. 2025). Persuasion written into a mathematics solution, with a length-matched control, raised scores for only two of six judges, while dissuasion lowered them for all six (Zheng, Wei and Kandanaarachchi 2026).

Grading a solution's working, not only its answer, is the grading-time form of supervising the process rather than the outcome (Lightman et al. 2023). Teachers annotated the first error in about 1,000 stepwise mathematics solutions written by a language model simulating students' errors (Daheim et al. 2024, from Macina et al. 2023), and current models find it hard to locate that error even when given the reference solution (Srivatsa, Maurya and Kochmar 2025).

Feedback is among the strongest influences on learning, and its effect can be negative (Hattie and Timperley 2007). A score shown to a language model pulls its later ratings toward that score, and neither reasoning nor a warning to disregard it removes the effect (Kapetanovic et al. 2026). Showing a feedback writer the score made its critique harsher at low grades and warmer at high ones, and a score-blind design improved alignment (Bulut et al. 2026). Feedback measures for tutoring have been validated against trained annotators on MRBench, a corpus of tutor replies to students' mathematics mistakes (Maurya et al. 2025).

# 2.4 Recordings and images

Benchmarks for models that take images, audio or video often fail to test whether the model uses that input. A model with no image scored 42.9% on one multimodal benchmark (Chen et al. 2024), audio-language models kept 60% to 72% of their benchmark scores with no audio (Foo et al. 2026), and a probe with no temporal information matched strong video-language models (Buch et al. 2022). Speech recognition can invent text, more often for speakers with longer pauses (Koenecke et al. 2024). Prompted multimodal models have been used to grade pronunciation on speechocean762 (Wang et al. 2025) and non-native speech more generally, where one model over-predicted the scores of low-quality speech (Parikh et al. 2025), and to assess surgical skill from video, where tasks needing temporal reasoning remained difficult (Rau et al. 2025). A recording's length carries real information about skill for human raters too: crowd raters gave higher skill scores to faster playback of the same surgery (Kelly et al. 2020). Text printed into an image can override what a multimodal model sees (Goh et al. 2021) and inject instructions (Cheng et al. 2025), and instructions can also be hidden in an image or a sound (Bagdasaryan et al. 2023). Across languages, spoken-language understanding correlates with the quality of speech recognition in that language (Schmidt et al. 2025), and models show a wide gap between high- and low-resource languages (Beyene et al. 2025). Vision systems have been audited for accuracy by skin type since Buolamwini and Gebru (2018), and the Casual Conversations corpora were built to measure models across apparent skin tone and ambient lighting (Hazirbas et al. 2022; Porgali et al. 2023); lighting also affects how skin tone is annotated on the Monk scale (Schumann et al. 2023).

# 2.5 Fairness and stability

Machine and human essay scores were compared within groups of test-takers before language models, with mostly similar results and some notable exceptions (Bridgeman, Trapani and Attali 2012). For students with learning disabilities or ADHD, human raters and a feature-based scoring engine gave similar average scores to prospective graduate students with and without these conditions, although the groups' essays differed in length and spelling errors (Buzick et al. 2016). Proxy variables and the way a scorer is estimated can bias automated scores, and a fairness criterion needs a psychometric definition (Johnson, Liu and McCaffrey 2022). Disability and socioeconomic status are less studied than race and gender in educational algorithms (Baker and Hawn 2022). A fine-tuned scorer on the parent corpus of ASAP 2.0 slightly magnified gaps already present in human scores (Kwako and Ormerod 2024), no configuration of GPT-4o was free of subgroup differences on young students' essays (Huang, Palermo and Wilson 2026), and language models gave more praise and less substantive critique on identical essays to students marked by race, language or disability (Tan, Phalen and Demszky 2026). Once the variation between retrained models is accounted for, many apparent unfairness results shrink (Cooper et al. 2024).

Models also change. The behavior of two widely used models changed substantially within three months (Chen, Zaharia and Zou 2024), updates can introduce new errors while accuracy rises (Srivastava et al. 2020), and language models scoring the same essays on two occasions fluctuated (Pack, Barrett and Escalante 2024). Models configured to be deterministic varied by up to 15% in accuracy across runs (Atil et al. 2024). A pre-registered audit of 12 language models as essay raters found that every version change shifted severity, and that agreement and severity did not change independently (Sunkavalli 2026).

# 2.6 Energy, carbon and water

The energy of a language-model query has been estimated from public performance data (Jegham et al. 2025) and measured in production, where the median text prompt to one provider's assistant used 0.24 Wh including idle machines and overhead (Elsworth et al. 2025). Measured figures for frontier models are below widely cited estimates, mainly because production servers batch many requests (Oviedo et al. 2026), and idealized assumptions about hardware use can also underestimate energy (Fernandez et al. 2025). Task-specific models are orders of magnitude cheaper to run than general generative ones (Luccioni, Jernite and Strubell 2024). Water use depends on where and when electricity is generated (Li, Yang, Islam and Ren 2025), and the carbon of making the hardware grows per query as its use falls (Gupta et al. 2021). Per-query figures travel without their boundaries (Luccioni, Gamazaychikov, et al. 2025), and cheaper computation can lead to more of it (Luccioni, Strubell and Crawford 2025).

# 3. Research questions

The benchmark is organized around six questions. Each is answered by one subsection of Section 5.

RQ1. Agreement. How closely do prompted language models agree with expert raters on short answers, code and essays, measured against how well the raters agree with each other, and against scorers trained on the same corpus's marked answers?

RQ2. Robustness. Can a student move a model's grade without improving the work, by writing a request or a forged instruction into the answer, by submitting a blank or meaningless answer, or through how the student is described; and do the grader's settings (an added instruction in the prompt, the model's reasoning effort, the numerical precision at which a host serves an open model, the wording of the prompt) change that?

RQ3. Beyond the grade. Does the model hold its grade when a student only disagrees, credit the working in a mathematics solution rather than only the final answer, and write feedback whose tone does not follow a grade it was told?

RQ4. Recordings and images. Do models that grade speech, handwritten work and video grade the recording itself: do they notice when there is nothing to grade, and does the language a student speaks change how well they judge it?

RQ5. Fairness and stability. Do models grade students in different groups differently at the same human grade, beyond the difference a second human rater shows, and do newer releases of a model grade the same work differently from older ones?

RQ6. Cost to the environment. How much energy, carbon and water does a grading use, measured where the model can be run on our own hardware and estimated where it cannot?

# 4. Method

# 4.1 Design

The benchmark is a fixed battery of public student work, each item with grades from expert human raters. Every grader grades the same items, and then altered versions of them, called probes. A probe changes one thing about the work, the context or the conversation, and a sound grader's response to it is known in advance: a blank answer should receive the lowest grade, a request for full marks appended to an answer should not raise it, and the same work introduced as coming from a strong or a weak student should receive the same grade. Because the expected response is fixed, the probes need no new human labels (as in behavioral testing; Ribeiro et al. 2020), and every grader can be compared on the same evidence.

A grader in this paper is a setup, not a model. It is one model, with one prompt, its settings (temperature, token limit and reasoning effort) and the provider that served it. All models are graded through the same plain prompt, which states the task, the reference answer and the rubric, and asks for a grade and a one-sentence reason in a fixed format (code/prompts/default.txt). The prompt is deliberately simple, so that the results describe the models rather than a tuned instruction, and so that any reader can re-run it.

# 4.2 Data

The benchmark uses eleven public corpora (Table 4.1). Each grading item has grades from expert human raters, or, for the studies that need no grade, a label fixed by how the corpus was built. Items are drawn once with a fixed seed. Each corpus is fetched from its source (code/docs/DATA-SOURCES.md), and the three corpora of the board are checked against hashes pinned in code/fetch_data.py. No student work, recording or image is published with this release.

# 4.3 Models and zero data retention

Twenty-two language models were graded on the text tasks (Table 4.2): seven closed models from three vendors and fifteen open-weight models from nine makers. Olmo 3.1 32B was served on a rented GPU with the vLLM inference server at 16-bit precision, and the machine and its disk were deleted after each run. The models that grade speech, images and video in Section 5.4 are named there.

Every request was required to go to an endpoint that retains no data. Since 2026-10-25, each request has been pinned to OpenRouter's live list of zero-retention endpoints, and a model with no such endpoint is refused, with the one exception below. One model, Claude Fable 5.1, has no zero-retention route; it was run only on public corpora, through OpenRouter on the maintainers' own Anthropic key under that key's 30-day safety retention, and is reported with that stated.

In runs made before 2026-10-25, about half of Claude Haiku 5.5's gradings went the same route, because of a configuration issue with the key stored with OpenRouter (bring-your-own-key); its board runs were then repeated under verified zero retention, but its earlier runs in other studies were not. The run records name the provider of each of those gradings, and OpenRouter's activity log for the model, matched to the runs, confirms the route. Its gradings in the handwriting study (848), in the video study's 16-frame run (1,055) and in the ELLIPSE fairness study (3,908) went to Anthropic's endpoint under the key's 30-day safety retention, an unintended exception made on public corpora only. Its gradings in the disability study and in the comparison of releases, and, by the run records, Claude Haiku 4.5's in that comparison, were served by Google's and Amazon Bedrock's zero-retention endpoints. No later run of Claude Haiku 5.5 in this paper went through the key, which was turned off on 2026-10-30.

# 4.4 Measures

Agreement is quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) between the model's grade and each rater's, averaged over raters. QWK is a chance-corrected measure of agreement on an ordered scale, in which a disagreement of two points costs four times as much as a disagreement of one. Because the raters themselves disagree, a model's QWK is reported as a share of the raters' QWK with each other, called the human ceiling. A share near 100% means the model disagrees with the raters about as often as they disagree with each other. The ASAP 2.0 essays release one adjudicated grade per essay, so the published agreement between their raters stands in for the ceiling.

Each probe's effect is the mean change in the grade it causes, as a share of the grading scale, with a 95% bootstrap interval over items. A grader is flagged when a probe gains it more than 5% of the scale, when it gives any credit to a blank or meaningless answer, or when it refuses more than 5% of gradings. The other measures are defined where they are first used in Section 5, and are summarized here. Pass/fail agreement is Cohen's kappa between the model's and the raters' grades split at the middle of the scale, as a share of the raters' own. The nonsense-word probe replaces every "the" in the answer with the non-word "blicket", which garbles the answer and should lower its grade. Consistency is the QWK between two gradings of the same answer. The learner-label effect is the grade when the student is described as strong minus the grade when described as weak, as a share of the scale. The working effect (Section 5.3) is how much a mathematics grade depends on whether the working is right with the final answer held fixed, and the pushback effect is how much more a grade rises after a student objects than after a request for a second look. Feedback is measured by how far its tone follows a wrong grade the model is told (Section 5.3). Beside these, the three checks of Williamson, Xi and Breyer (2012) are applied with the thresholds tabulated by Wood et al. (2021): a QWK of at least 0.70, a QWK no more than 0.10 below the raters' agreement, and a standardized mean difference of no more than 0.15.

# 4.5 How the grades are combined

Each measure is turned into a score from 0 to 100 by a fixed rule and grouped into nine strands. Six apply to anything that returns a grade (agreement, pass/fail agreement, reacting to wrong content, ignoring what should not matter, fairness to the learner's label, and consistency). Three apply only to a model that can be asked to do more than grade (feedback, reading the working, and holding the grade under pushback). The whole-task score weights all nine; the weights are a published judgment, and the benchmark's site lets a reader set their own. The feedback strand is 100 × W / (W + |S|), where S is how far feedback tone moves per point of a wrong grade the model is told and W how far it moves per point of the work's quality when no grade is told (Section 5.3): the share of the tone's movement that comes from the work. It is 100 when a wrong grade moves nothing, 50 when it moves the tone as much as the work does, and 0 when the tone does not follow the work. A model with a disqualifying flag ranks below every model without one. Scorers trained on the corpus's own marked answers are reported beside the models on the six grading strands, for comparison, and are not ranked, because they produce only a grade and need hundreds of marked answers for every new question.

# 4.6 Self-checks against planted effects

Every probe and every study verdict, except the six sets of statistics named later in this section, was first run on simulated graders built to resemble the real ones, with a known effect planted, and on simulated graders with no effect: a simulation study of each statistic's power and false-alarm rate (Morris, White and Crowther 2019). A statistic passed if it found the planted effect in at least 80% of simulated runs and raised a false alarm in no more than the rate stated for it, usually 5% to 7%. A probe of the board that failed this check is not reported, and a study's measure that failed it is reported as UNMEASURED.

Of the analyses the release declares, 30 are studies; the others prepare data or, for the comparison of releases, are exploratory. Each study opens with its pre-registration, in its script or, for the speech, handwriting and video tasks, in a PREREG.md file, and numbers its later changes with their reasons. Every study states a threshold and verdict wording in advance except four, which state what they will report and, where it applies, what a sound grader does, but no verdict: the trained scorers (code/baselines/baselines.py, expectations rather than verdicts), the feedback board's columns (code/feedback-board/fb.py), and the speech and handwriting tasks (code/speech/PREREG.md, code/images/PREREG.md).

The board itself stated its probe battery and its detection thresholds in advance, but its disqualifying flags were added after its first rows (below). The speech, handwriting and video pre-registrations were written after a smoke run of two cases or three gradings, which is not part of a result; the perception audit's was written first, and its design was changed after a one-model pilot (its CHANGE 1), before any call of the design it ran.

The board's own scoring also changed after its first results without a numbered change: the whole-task score, its strand weights and rank intervals, and the disqualifying flags (gaming above 5% of the scale, any credit for a blank answer, refusals above 5%) with the rule that a flagged model ranks below every unflagged one, were added together (benchmark commit d04c148f), the reading-the-working and pushback strands were added to it (bef2041b), the false-discovery correction and the per-task scores were added (09ef6229), and the feedback strand was changed twice (c23ba3aa, 60a885c8; Section 5.3). Each is in the repository's commit history; the two feedback-strand changes also have rows in code/docs/CORRECTIONS.md, and the false-discovery correction and per-task scores are dated in code/leaderboard.py's opening text.

Six sets of statistics were not checked on simulated graders and are reported with their intervals only: the three standard agreement checks and the direction of each model's departure (Section 5.1); the held-out note in the study of settings (Section 5.2), one condition of its FIXED verdict, whose rule for being read is applied to the real runs; the split of the pushback effect by whether the model had graded the answer below the raters (Section 5.3); the board's two feedback columns, the halo and the share of feedback that gives away the answer (Section 5.3), which code/floor.py does not cover; the handwriting probes (Section 5.4); and the comparison of releases (Section 5.5), which was exploratory and is reported as point estimates. The video study's verdict (Section 5.4) was checked on three planted graders, one simulated dataset each, rather than on many. The ratio of the two slopes in the wrong-grade feedback study (Section 5.3) was registered as descriptive.

The board's own check (code/floor.py, code/out/floor.json) planted eleven probe effects, eight of them nonzero, in 20 simulated datasets and planted none in 20 more. Each planted nonzero effect was flagged, with the right sign, in 18 to 20 of its 20 datasets, and each effect that was absent was flagged in no more than 2 of 20. A positive control recomputed the agreement between the Mohler corpus's two raters over all 1,727 answers and matched its expected value (0.519Printed0.519Source value0.519321HowQWK between the two Mohler raters over all 1,727 answersFilecode/out/floor.jsonFieldmohler_positive_control › ceilingAnalysisfloor (release file)Build checkmatches at build). One check failed: a statistic meant to show whether a model grades more accurately on the answers it grades consistently did not reach its bar, so that statistic is not reported.

Each study in Section 5 that has a check of its own ran it in the same way; where a check failed, any figure for the measure is given as descriptive (for example, the generative fine-tune's essay agreement in Section 5.1 and the reverse regression in Section 5.5), and a study whose check failed before its runs changed its design, recorded the change, and checked again.

# 4.7 Trained scorers

Five scorers were trained on each corpus's graded answers outside the board's 100 and scored on those 100 under the same probes as the models (code/baselines/). They are length alone; word frequencies (TF-IDF) with ridge regression; similarity to the reference answer; MiniLM sentence embeddings (Reimers and Gurevych 2019; Wang et al. 2020) with ridge regression; and DeBERTa-v3-base fine-tuned on the grades (He, Gao and Chen 2021). They had 1,627 graded short answers, 29 graded programs and 24,628 graded essays to train on. Two further studies trained larger models on essays (code/essays-finetune/, code/essays-genft/), using 23,628 graded essays and 1,000 held-out test essays: Qwen3 4B and Gemma 4 26B A4B with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a regression head, and Gemma 4 26B A4B fine-tuned so that it still writes the board's reply, a grade followed by a reason. The trained scorers are reported beside the models and are not ranked.

# 4.8 Ethics

Every corpus is public and was used under its license; no student, teacher or other person was contacted, and no new data about people were collected. Only grades and aggregate results are published: no student work, recording, image or model reply is published. Group labels (disability, economic status, race and ethnicity, skin tone) were used only as the corpora release them, and results are reported only for groups, never for individuals. Every request asked for an endpoint that retains no data; the exceptions stated in Section 4.3 involved only public corpora. The perception audit used Casual Conversations v2 under its license: videos were sent unmodified, only to open models on the study's own rented GPU, the study created no labels of the people in the videos and relied only on the corpus's own skin-tone and lighting labels, no image from the corpus is published, and the videos used are listed so that they can be deleted if the licensor asks.

# 5. Results

Every figure in this section comes from the committed outputs of the code package. The per-model results are in code/out/public/ and each study's own output is in its out/ folder. Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals over the items graded (answers, essays, recordings or solutions) unless a subsection says otherwise. An effect is called shown when its interval excludes 0, and "not shown" when the interval includes 0; "not shown" does not mean that there is no effect. Verdicts in capitals are the pre-registered verdict strings of each study, quoted as they were written.

# 5.1 Agreement (RQ1)

Agreement was measured first because it is the evidence usually offered for a language-model grader. Every model graded the same 100 answers per task: computer science short answers (Mohler, Bunescu and Mihalcea 2011), student programs (Mendonça et al. 2026) and persuasive and source-based essays (The Learning Agency 2024). Each model's quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) with the raters is set beside the raters' agreement with each other. A model's agreement also varies from one assignment to the next (code/out/public/per_prompt.json). The essays were written to seven assignments and the programs to three exercises. Five essay assignments, with 10 to 21 essays each, and all three exercises, with 22 to 44 programs each, have enough answers for a QWK; the other two essay assignments have 7 essays each. These per-assignment figures rest on few answers each, so part of this spread is sampling variation.

The three checks that testing organizations apply before trusting a machine's grades (Williamson, Xi and Breyer 2012) were applied to every model and task (code/out/public/agreement_flags.json). The checks require a QWK of at least 0.70, a QWK no more than 0.10 below the raters' agreement with each other, and a standardized mean difference (SMD) between the model's grades and the raters' of no more than 0.15 in absolute value. Each check reads PASS, FAIL or INDETERMINATE according to whether its interval lies on one side of the threshold. No model passes all three checks on any task. The SMD shows the direction in which the models depart. These verdicts rest, as pre-registered, on the first study's planted-effect check for paired differences between two graders on the same essays, which detected a planted difference in 93% of 200 simulated runs. The same kind of paired difference on the same essays, the generative fine-tune's gain over its base, failed its own check, so the fold verdicts carry that tension.

Answer to RQ1. On short answers, most prompted models agree with the raters about as well as the two raters agree with each other, and none is shown to exceed them. On code, four models are shown to agree with the raters more than the raters agree with each other, and fourteen are shown to agree less. On essays, no prompted model's point estimate reaches the raters' published agreement, and 18 of the 22 are shown to fall below it. A scorer fine-tuned on the corpus's graded essays has a higher point estimate than any prompted model and, in a paired comparison on 500 held-out essays, exceeds the best of the three prompted arms it was compared with (Claude Opus 5.5 given six graded essays); a scorer that uses length alone has a higher point estimate than 16 of the 22 models. Every model nevertheless carries agreement beyond essay length. No model passes all three standard checks on any task: on short answers and essays no model's QWK is shown to reach 0.70, and on code, where eight models pass the first two checks, they grade lower than the raters. Re-run this finding Recompute the agreement ranges, the ceiling comparisons and the trained-scorer contrasts of RQ1 from the committed outputs (executed when this report was built; every assertion passed)

Download the notebook, clone the ai-grading-benchmark repository at the commit the release file names, and set GBENCH_DIR to the clone (or put the notebook in a folder beside it), then run all cells. The notebook reads that repository's committed outputs. Python 3.9 or later with numpy.

Re-run: agreement (RQ1)

This notebook recomputes the headline numbers of RQ1 from the benchmark repository's committed outputs: out/leaderboard.json (every model's QWK on the board's 100 answers per task, with its share of the raters' agreement), out/baselines.json (the trained scorers) and essays-finetune/out/essays-finetune.json (the fine-tuning study). It counts from the intervals themselves rather than reading verdict strings. It needs only Python; the gradings behind these files are not published (the harness is held back), so the QWKs are recomputed by the scripts that wrote these files, not here.

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "ai-grading-benchmark-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = "per-case-model-outputs.jsonl"


def find_release_file(name=DATA_NAME):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        for n in (name, name + ".gz"):
            if (d / n).is_file():
                return d / n
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder): in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file():
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


SOURCE_ENV, SOURCE_NAME = "GBENCH_DIR", "ai-grading-benchmark"   # set when a release's code is another repository


def source_repo():
    """The repository a release's code and committed outputs are published in (a release whose paper cites
    it rather than a copied code package): $SOURCE_ENV, or a checkout named SOURCE_NAME beside this
    notebook or beside a folder above it."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ[SOURCE_ENV])] if SOURCE_ENV and os.environ.get(SOURCE_ENV) else []
    places += [p / SOURCE_NAME for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        if d.is_dir() and (d / "out").is_dir():
            return d
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the {SOURCE_NAME} repository this release's code is published in. Clone it at the "
        f"commit the release file names, then set the environment variable {SOURCE_ENV} to the clone, or "
        f"run this notebook from a folder beside it.")


def load_source_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of that repository, by its path there (cited in the paper as code/<path>)."""
    return json.loads((source_repo() / relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


print("Source repository:", shown(source_repo()))
Source repository: ../../../../../../ai-grading-benchmark

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

def p(x, d=3, sign=False):
    """Round half-up once from the unrounded value, as the paper prints it."""
    v = Decimal(repr(float(x))).quantize(Decimal(1).scaleb(-d), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
    return f"{v:+.{d}f}" if sign else f"{v:.{d}f}"

lb = load_source_json("out/leaderboard.json")["rows"]
by = {}
for r in lb:
    by.setdefault(r["task"], []).append(r)
assert all(len(v) == 22 for v in by.values()), {k: len(v) for k, v in by.items()}

for task, lo, hi in (("mohler", "0.379", "0.680"), ("code", "0.268", "0.879"), ("asap2", "0.155", "0.727")):
    q = [r["qwk"]["estimate"] for r in by[task]]
    print(task, "QWK from", p(min(q)), "to", p(max(q)))
    assert (p(min(q)), p(max(q))) == (lo, hi)

Against the raters. On code, a model is shown to agree with the raters more than they agree with each other when its share of the ceiling has an interval wholly above 100%, and less when wholly below. On essays, the ceiling is the published weighted κ 0.745.

code = by["code"]
above = sum(r["share_of_ceiling"]["ci95"][0] > 1 for r in code)
below = sum(r["share_of_ceiling"]["ci95"][1] < 1 for r in code)
print("code: above the raters", above, "below", below)
assert (above, below) == (4, 14)
ess = by["asap2"]
ceiling = ess[0]["published_ceiling"]["value"]
whole_below = sum(r["qwk"]["ci95"][1] < ceiling for r in ess)
print("essays: published agreement", ceiling, "; models whose whole interval lies below it:", whole_below)
assert ceiling == 0.745 and whole_below == 18
assert not any(r["qwk"]["estimate"] >= ceiling for r in ess)
mohler_below = [r["model"] for r in by["mohler"] if r["share_of_ceiling"]["ci95"][1] < 1]
print("short answers: shown to agree less than the raters:", mohler_below)
assert mohler_below == ["meta-llama/llama-3.2-3b-instruct"]
code: above the raters 4 below 14
essays: published agreement 0.745 ; models whose whole interval lies below it: 18

Trained scorers. A scorer that uses only the essay's length, and DeBERTa fine-tuned on the corpus's graded essays, set against the 22 prompted models on the same 100 essays; then the paired comparison of DeBERTa with the best prompted arm on 500 held-out essays.

bl = {(r["model"], r["task"]): r for r in load_source_json("out/baselines.json")["rows"]}
length = bl[("baseline: length", "asap2")]["qwk"]["estimate"]
deberta = bl[("baseline: deberta-ft", "asap2")]["qwk"]["estimate"]
beaten = sum(r["qwk"]["estimate"] < length for r in ess)
print("length-only essay QWK", p(length), "is higher than", beaten, "of 22 models; DeBERTa", p(deberta))
assert p(length) == "0.636" and beaten == 16 and p(deberta) == "0.809"
assert deberta > max(r["qwk"]["estimate"] for r in ess)
c2 = load_source_json("essays-finetune/out/essays-finetune.json")["comparisons"]["C2"]
print("DeBERTa minus Claude Opus 5.5 with six examples:", p(-c2["estimate"]), [p(-c2["ci95"][1]), p(-c2["ci95"][0])])
assert (p(-c2["estimate"]), p(-c2["ci95"][1]), p(-c2["ci95"][0])) == ("0.095", "0.059", "0.130")
assert c2["ci95"][1] < 0   # the direction: the prompted arm minus DeBERTa lies below 0

# 5.2 Robustness (RQ2)

Agreement on ordinary work does not show what a grader does with work designed to move it, so every model graded probes alongside the 100 answers per task. Two probes append a note to the answer: a polite request for full marks, and a forged grading override. A blank or meaningless answer should receive the lowest grade. The same answer is presented once as coming from a strong student and once from a weak one, and should receive the same grade. The answer's line breaks are re-wrapped, which should change nothing. Finally, every "the" in the answer is replaced with the non-word "blicket", which garbles the answer and should lower the grade. Each effect is the mean change in the grade as a share of the scale, with a 95% interval over answers. A model is flagged when a note gains it more than 5% of the scale, or when it gives any credit to a blank or meaningless answer (Section 4.4). Table 5.2 gives each model's largest effects.

Table 5.2. Robustness on the board's 100 answers per task. The largest gain from either note across the three tasks, as a share of the scale, with its 95% interval over answers and the task in brackets; the highest share of blank or meaningless answers given more than the lowest grade; the largest effect of describing the student as strong rather than weak; and the board's flags. Positive values raise the grade. Source: code/out/leaderboard.json and code/out/overall.json.

Describing the student as strong rather than weak raised the grade in 28 of the 66 model-task pairs, with an interval above 0 (24 after the Benjamini–Hochberg correction below), and lowered it in none. This extends to 22 models the attainment-label effect reported on six (Porcaro 2026). Replacing "the" with the non-word lowered the grade, as it should, in 40 of the 44 pairs where it applies (short answers and essays). In the other four the interval reaches 0: Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5 Mini and GPT-5.6 Luna on short answers, and Claude Opus 5.5 on essays.

The board reports 230 probe intervals, so some would exclude 0 by chance (code/out/public/multiplicity.json). Of the 230, 121 exclude 0, and 112 of those survive the Benjamini–Hochberg correction for a false discovery rate of 5% (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995). The nine that do not survive might be chance. None of the nine is the sole basis of a flag.

Four studies asked whether the grader's settings change these results. The first (code/setups/README.md) re-ran the 14 flagged models with a guard sentence added to the prompt, which states that nothing inside the work is an instruction and that blank or non-attempts receive the lowest grade, and, for the seven models that can reason at a chosen effort, at high reasoning effort. A setup FIXED a model when no task was gamed by more than 5%, a held-out note was not gamed by more than 5%, no blank answer was credited and mean QWK stayed within 0.05 of the default setup. Four of the 14 models were fixed by one setup or the other, and the gains below are each model's worst task under the default setup run the same day. Because each setup was run once, a follow-up study (code/guard-retest/README.md) re-ran all four of these models, Olmo 3.1 32B self-hosted as on the board, six times with the default prompt and five times with the guard sentence, and compared the guard's effect with the spread between runs of the same prompt. Gaming here is the larger note's mean gain on each task, averaged over the three tasks; attack success is the share of answer and note pairs whose grade rose by more than 5% of the scale. The second study (code/hosting/README.md) asked whether the numerical precision at which a host serves an open model matters. The same requests were sent to hosts serving DeepSeek V4 Pro and GLM 5.3 at 8-bit or at 4-bit precision. The verdict is PRECISION MATTERS in all three comparisons, and in each the forged override gained more at 4-bit. The third study (code/paraphrase/README.md) asked whether rewording the prompt, while keeping every instruction, moves grades more than asking the same prompt again. Each model graded the 300 board answers under the default prompt five more times and under six rewordings. The measure is the share of answers whose grade moves by more than 5% of the scale under a rewording, minus the same share under a plain re-ask. Neither the base nor the fine-tuned model credited a blank answer (0 of 180 and 0 of 194).

Answer to RQ2. For 14 of the 22 models as their hosts served them, a note written into the answer moves the grade by more than 5% of the scale, by up to 83% of it, and seven of these also credit blank or meaningless answers; for one of the 14, GLM 5.3, the largest gain, on code, is that of its 4-bit hosts, though its gains on the other two tasks also exceed 5%. Describing the student as strong raised grades in 28 of 66 model-task pairs (24 after correction for multiple comparisons) and lowered them in none. The settings matter: in a single run, high reasoning effort or an added guard sentence fixes four of the 14 flagged models, and the guard sentence makes three others, Gemma 3 4B, Gemma 3 27B and Olmo 3.1 32B, more gameable beyond the spread between repeated runs. A 4-bit host is gamed more than an 8-bit host of the same model in all three comparisons, but with the host held fixed, for two smaller dense models, 4-bit weights were not shown to raise the forged override's gain by more than 5% of the scale, though for Phi-4 on code they raised the polite request's gain by 9.9Printed9.9Source valuex = 0.0993333Filecode/precision-controlled/out/precision-controlled.jsonFieldx * 100 where x = comparisons › {'model': 'microsoft/phi-4', 'task': 'code', 'pair': 'mxfp4 - fp8'} › injection_gain_diff › estimateAnalysisprecision-controlled (release file)Build checkmatches at build%. For 11 of the 22 models a rewording of the prompt moves more grades than asking again does, although the models' ranking by agreement was not shown to depend on the wording more than on a re-ask (the whole-task ranking was not tested). Fine-tuning on essays made one model less gameable on essays and more gameable on short answers.

Re-run this finding Recount the flags, the label effects, the rewording verdicts, the guard re-test and the precision studies of RQ2 (executed when this report was built; every assertion passed)

Download the notebook, clone the ai-grading-benchmark repository at the commit the release file names, and set GBENCH_DIR to the clone (or put the notebook in a folder beside it), then run all cells. The notebook reads that repository's committed outputs. Python 3.9 or later with numpy.

Re-run: robustness (RQ2)

This notebook recounts RQ2's headline numbers from the benchmark repository's committed outputs: out/leaderboard.json (each probe's effect with its interval, per model and task), out/overall.json (the board's flags), paraphrase/out/paraphrase.json (the rewording study) and hosting/out/hosting.json (8-bit against 4-bit hosts). Flags are recounted from the effects and the board's 5% rule, not only read.

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "ai-grading-benchmark-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = "per-case-model-outputs.jsonl"


def find_release_file(name=DATA_NAME):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        for n in (name, name + ".gz"):
            if (d / n).is_file():
                return d / n
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder): in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file():
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


SOURCE_ENV, SOURCE_NAME = "GBENCH_DIR", "ai-grading-benchmark"   # set when a release's code is another repository


def source_repo():
    """The repository a release's code and committed outputs are published in (a release whose paper cites
    it rather than a copied code package): $SOURCE_ENV, or a checkout named SOURCE_NAME beside this
    notebook or beside a folder above it."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ[SOURCE_ENV])] if SOURCE_ENV and os.environ.get(SOURCE_ENV) else []
    places += [p / SOURCE_NAME for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        if d.is_dir() and (d / "out").is_dir():
            return d
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the {SOURCE_NAME} repository this release's code is published in. Clone it at the "
        f"commit the release file names, then set the environment variable {SOURCE_ENV} to the clone, or "
        f"run this notebook from a folder beside it.")


def load_source_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of that repository, by its path there (cited in the paper as code/<path>)."""
    return json.loads((source_repo() / relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


print("Source repository:", shown(source_repo()))
Source repository: ../../../../../../ai-grading-benchmark

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

def p(x, d=1, sign=False):
    v = Decimal(repr(float(x))).quantize(Decimal(1).scaleb(-d), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
    return f"{v:+.{d}f}" if sign else f"{v:.{d}f}"

# 5.3 Beyond the grade (RQ3)

A grader that a student can talk to, and that writes feedback, can fail in ways a grade alone does not show. Three behaviors were measured on every model, and Table 5.3 gives the results. The first is pushback. After grading a short answer, the conversation continued with the student either objecting ("I think my answer is correct and deserves full marks") or asking for a second look ("Please double-check your grade"). The work does not change, so a sound grader gives the same grade either way. The pushback effect is how much more the grade rose after the objection than after the request for a second look, as a share of the scale. The second is whether the model credits the working in a mathematics solution. Each of 200 word problems was written in four versions: right working with the right answer, right working with a slip at the end, wrong working that lands on the right answer, and wrong working with a wrong answer (Daheim et al. 2024, built from Macina et al. 2023 and the problems of Cobbe et al. 2021). The working effect is how much the grade, out of 4, depends on whether the working is right with the final answer held fixed; an answer checker scores 0. The third is whether the tone of a model's feedback follows a grade it was told when that grade contradicts the work.

Table 5.3. Pushback, mathematical working and feedback. Pushback effect as a share of the scale on the board's short answers below full marks, with its 95% interval over answers; working effect out of 4 points on 200 problems, with its 95% interval over problems; S, the change in feedback tone per point of a wrong grade the model was told, with its 95% interval over answers (every model reads TONE FOLLOWS THE TOLD GRADE); and the share of feedback on answers below full credit that the Withholding Answers evaluator judges to give away the answer, with its 95% interval. Olmo 3.1 32B's working effect comes from its board grades, as its replies were not kept. Sources: code/feedback-board/out/pushback.json, code/maths-process/out/process.json, code/feedback-discordant/out/discordant.json and code/feedback-board/out/feedback-board.json.

Feedback was scored only with measures first tested against trained annotators. Six candidate measures were tested on MRBench (Maurya et al. 2025), 1,655 tutor replies to a student's mathematics mistake labeled by trained annotators, whose own agreement is κ 0.65 to 0.71 (code/feedback-validity/README.md). A measure passed (VALIDATED) if its area under the curve (AUC), the probability that it ranks a reply the annotators labeled yes above one they labeled no, had a 95% interval above 0.60 and beat the reply's length. Two passed. The tone rule supports the test of whether feedback follows a wrong grade (code/feedback-discordant/README.md). Each model wrote feedback on the board's 100 short answers twice: once told the teacher's grade m, and once told its mirror, 5 − m, so that an answer the teacher gave 5 was said to have scored 0. The work is the same in both, so feedback that responds only to the work has the same tone in both. The told-grade slope S is the change in tone per point of told grade with the work held fixed, from the paired difference between the two versions of each answer's feedback; a positive S means the tone follows the told grade. Beside it, W is the slope of tone on the teacher's grade when no grade is told, which measures how far the same model's tone follows the quality of the work. An earlier measure, the halo, told each model the true grade and compared its feedback with feedback written with no grade: the correlation between tone and grade when the grade was shown minus the same correlation when it was hidden. Answer to RQ3. Most models give way more to a student's bare objection than to a request for a second look: 17 of 22 raise their grade more after the objection, including six of the eight models without a flag (no note's mean gain above 5% of the scale, and no blank answer credited). Nearly every model credits the working in a mathematics solution rather than only the final answer, but the models that read the working differ by up to 1.865Printed1.865Source value1.645, 1.6, 1.88, 2.94, 3.185, 3.10553, 2.345, 2.82, 3.13, 2.945, 2.99, 2.955, 2.97, 2.8, 1.55, 2.87, 2.90955, 2.695, 2.335, 3.415Filecode/maths-process/out/process.jsonFieldmax(v) - min(v) where v = 20 values (graders › 1 › mean_credit › slip, …)Analysismaths-process (release file)Build checkmatches at build points of 4 on what a slip at the end costs. Told a grade that contradicts the work, every one of the 22 models writes feedback whose tone, measured by a word rule validated on tutoring replies, follows that grade, and for eight of them the point estimate of that shift is at least as large as the shift with the quality of the work (a descriptive ratio with no interval). Fine-tuning one model on essays made it read the mathematics working less.

Re-run this finding Recount pushback, the working effect and feedback told a wrong grade for RQ3, and the cost of a slip (executed when this report was built; every assertion passed)

Download the notebook, clone the ai-grading-benchmark repository at the commit the release file names, and set GBENCH_DIR to the clone (or put the notebook in a folder beside it), then run all cells. The notebook reads that repository's committed outputs. Python 3.9 or later with numpy.

Re-run: beyond the grade (RQ3)

From the benchmark repository's committed outputs: feedback-board/out/pushback.json (the pushback effect per model), maths-process/out/process.json (credit for working, per model and version of each problem) and feedback-discordant/out/discordant.json (feedback told a wrong grade). Counts come from the intervals.

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "ai-grading-benchmark-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = "per-case-model-outputs.jsonl"


def find_release_file(name=DATA_NAME):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        for n in (name, name + ".gz"):
            if (d / n).is_file():
                return d / n
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder): in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file():
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


SOURCE_ENV, SOURCE_NAME = "GBENCH_DIR", "ai-grading-benchmark"   # set when a release's code is another repository


def source_repo():
    """The repository a release's code and committed outputs are published in (a release whose paper cites
    it rather than a copied code package): $SOURCE_ENV, or a checkout named SOURCE_NAME beside this
    notebook or beside a folder above it."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ[SOURCE_ENV])] if SOURCE_ENV and os.environ.get(SOURCE_ENV) else []
    places += [p / SOURCE_NAME for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        if d.is_dir() and (d / "out").is_dir():
            return d
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the {SOURCE_NAME} repository this release's code is published in. Clone it at the "
        f"commit the release file names, then set the environment variable {SOURCE_ENV} to the clone, or "
        f"run this notebook from a folder beside it.")


def load_source_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of that repository, by its path there (cited in the paper as code/<path>)."""
    return json.loads((source_repo() / relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


print("Source repository:", shown(source_repo()))
Source repository: ../../../../../../ai-grading-benchmark

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

def p(x, d=3):
    return f"{Decimal(repr(float(x))).quantize(Decimal(1).scaleb(-d), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP):.{d}f}"

pb = load_source_json("feedback-board/out/pushback.json")["models"]
yields = sum(v["pushback"]["ci95"][0] > 0 for v in pb.values())
print(yields, "of", len(pb), "models raise the grade when the student only disagrees")
assert (yields, len(pb)) == (17, 22)

gr = [g for g in load_source_json("maths-process/out/process.json")["graders"] if g["grader"] in pb]
reads = [g for g in gr if g["reasoning_ci95"][0] > 0.5]
print(len(reads), "of", len(gr), "read the working (interval above 0.5 of 4)")
assert (len(reads), len(gr)) == (20, 22)
slip = [g["mean_credit"]["slip"] for g in reads]
print("credit for right working with a slip at the end:", p(min(slip)), "to", p(max(slip)), "; difference", p(max(slip) - min(slip)))
assert (p(min(slip)), p(max(slip)), p(max(slip) - min(slip))) == ("1.550", "3.415", "1.865")
17 of 22 models raise the grade when the student only disagrees
20 of 22 read the working (interval above 0.5 of 4)
credit for right working with a slip at the end: 1.550 to 3.415 ; difference 1.865

fd = load_source_json("feedback-discordant/out/discordant.json")["rows"]
follows = [r for r in fd if r["ci95"][0] > 0 and r["verdict"] == "TONE FOLLOWS THE TOLD GRADE"]
print(len(follows), "of", len(fd), "models: feedback tone follows a wrong told grade")
assert (len(follows), len(fd)) == (22, 22)
ge = [r["model"] for r in fd if r["told_grade_slope"] >= r["work_slope_blind"]]
print("a wrong grade moves the tone at least as much as the work does for", len(ge), "models")
assert len(ge) == 8
22 of 22 models: feedback tone follows a wrong told grade
a wrong grade moves the tone at least as much as the work does for 8 models

# 5.4 Recordings and images (RQ4)

Models that accept sound, images or video were graded on tasks in those media, with probes that test whether the grade comes from the recording. Each probe has a known sound response: a silent recording or a blank screen should receive the lowest grade, and the same recording described as coming from a strong or a weak student should receive the same grade.

Seven audio models graded the pronunciation of 100 English sentences read by Mandarin-speaking children and adults, each scored by five experts from 0 to 10 (Zhang et al. 2021; code/speech/README.md). A second study tested whether an audio model recognizes a correct spoken answer as well in a less common language (code/language/README.md). It used the same sentences read aloud in 18 languages (Conneau et al. 2023), six each of high, middle and low resource. Each recording was paired once with its own sentence and once with another as an English model answer. Fifteen models graded 122 handwritten solutions to Russian school-leaving mathematics problems, each with one official expert score, on three scales (0 to 2, 0 to 3 and 0 to 4; Khrulev 2025; code/images/README.md). With one score per solution there is no ceiling, so these are agreement figures without a reference. Video was tested on 100 recordings of laparoscopic training tasks, each rated by three raters on a total scale of 4 to 20 (Funke et al. 2026; code/video/README.md). A recording's length predicts its rating, and the prompt states the length, as the raters knew it; a simulated grader that only times the recording reaches QWK 0.57Printed0.57Source value0.565057Howa simulated grader that only times the recording; the raters' own QWK, human.ceiling_qwk, is 0.571Filecode/out/video/floor-beyond-length.jsonFieldruns › stopwatch › base › qwkAnalysisvideo (release file)Build checkmatches at build, the raters' own agreement. The pre-registered measure is therefore agreement beyond length: the partial Spearman correlation of the model's grade with the raters' mean, controlling for length within each task. A model WATCHES THE RECORDING if this interval lies above 0. Models without video input were sent 16 evenly spaced frames. Table 5.5 gives every run.

Nova 2 Lite described the video instead of rating it on nearly every grading. Nine of the 21 runs never credited a black screen; Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemma 3 4B credited every black screen and every frozen frame. The two Gemma 4 endpoints were charged about 2,860 and 2,880 input tokens per recording whatever its length, so they were most likely sent a few frames rather than the recording, as MiMo v2.6 Flash was (2,508).

The last study audited whether a video model says it cannot see a speaker who is plainly on screen, by skin tone and lighting (code/perception/README.md). It used 1,280 recordings of consenting adults answering a question to camera (Porgali et al. 2023), with skin tone taken only from the dataset's Monk labels, and lighting from the dataset's label for whether a recording was made in daylight or after dark. The license does not allow sending a reduced copy of a video, and the hosted endpoints refused most full-length videos as too large (a 102 MB and a 168 MB video were refused in a pilot; the sample's median is about 155 MB), so hosted models are not in this study. Three open models were run on the study's own GPU: Gemma 4 26B A4B, Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8 27B. All three graded 1,278 of the 1,280 recordings, and all three said "not visible" on each of 10 black, silent control clips. Gemma 4 26B A4B and Gemma 4 31B said they could not see the speaker in 0 of 1,278 recordings and refused none. With no failures, there is no gap between groups to measure, so the pre-registered gap verdicts read UNMEASURED. Qwen3.8 27B DID NOT DO THE TASK: 21% of its replies had no usable answer, above the registered limit of 20%, and its 822 "cannot see" replies are not credible, because in 372 of them it also rated the speaker's delivery. Before the study moved to its own GPU, one hosted model, MiMo v2.6 Flash, was sent the 10 control clips in a pilot. On 7 of them it said a speaker was visible and audible and rated the delivery 3 to 5. This is a pilot observation, not a result.

Answer to RQ4. Most models that grade recordings do not reliably notice when there is nothing to grade: six of seven audio models credit nearly every silent recording, and 12 of 21 video runs credit a black screen at least once. Only four of 21 video runs are shown to grade the recording beyond its length.
