Re-run this finding Recount the silence, black-screen and beyond-length results of RQ4, and the perception bounds (executed when this report was built; every assertion passed)

Download the notebook, clone the ai-grading-benchmark repository at the commit the release file names, and set GBENCH_DIR to the clone (or put the notebook in a folder beside it), then run all cells. The notebook reads that repository's committed outputs. Python 3.9 or later with numpy.

Re-run: recordings and images (RQ4)

From the benchmark repository's committed outputs: out/speech/*.json (each audio model's results), out/public/video.json (every video run), out/images/*.json (handwritten solutions on three scales), language/out/language.json and perception/out/perception.json. The perception bound is the one-sided 95% upper bound on a failure rate with no failures in n recordings, 1 − 0.05^(1/n).

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "ai-grading-benchmark-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = "per-case-model-outputs.jsonl"


def find_release_file(name=DATA_NAME):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        for n in (name, name + ".gz"):
            if (d / n).is_file():
                return d / n
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder): in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file():
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


SOURCE_ENV, SOURCE_NAME = "GBENCH_DIR", "ai-grading-benchmark"   # set when a release's code is another repository


def source_repo():
    """The repository a release's code and committed outputs are published in (a release whose paper cites
    it rather than a copied code package): $SOURCE_ENV, or a checkout named SOURCE_NAME beside this
    notebook or beside a folder above it."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ[SOURCE_ENV])] if SOURCE_ENV and os.environ.get(SOURCE_ENV) else []
    places += [p / SOURCE_NAME for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        if d.is_dir() and (d / "out").is_dir():
            return d
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the {SOURCE_NAME} repository this release's code is published in. Clone it at the "
        f"commit the release file names, then set the environment variable {SOURCE_ENV} to the clone, or "
        f"run this notebook from a folder beside it.")


def load_source_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of that repository, by its path there (cited in the paper as code/<path>)."""
    return json.loads((source_repo() / relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


print("Source repository:", shown(source_repo()))
Source repository: ../../../../../../ai-grading-benchmark

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP
from pathlib import Path

def p(x, d=1):
    return f"{Decimal(repr(float(x))).quantize(Decimal(1).scaleb(-d), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP):.{d}f}"

speech = [load_source_json(f"out/speech/{f.name}") for f in sorted((source_repo() / "out/speech").glob("speech-*.json"))]
sil = [s["validity"]["null_answers"]["by_kind"]["null_silence"]["credited"] for s in speech]
print("silent recordings credited:", [p(100 * x) for x in sil])
assert len(speech) == 7 and sum(float(p(100 * x)) >= 89.7 for x in sil) == 6   # 89.7% to 100%, as printed
lang = load_source_json("language/out/language.json")["models"]
worse = sum(m["gap_high_minus_low"]["ci95"][0] > 0 for m in lang)
print(worse, "of", len(lang), "audio models are worse on low-resource languages")
assert (worse, len(lang)) == (6, 7)
silent recordings credited: ['100.0', '100.0', '100.0', '5.0', '100.0', '96.7', '89.7']
6 of 7 audio models are worse on low-resource languages

runs = [v for v in load_source_json("out/public/video.json") if v["verdict"] != "REFERENCE"]
watches = sum(v["beyond_lo"] is not None and v["beyond_lo"] > 0 for v in runs)
black = sum(v["black_pct"] > 0 for v in runs)
print(len(runs), "video runs;", watches, "grade beyond length;", black, "credit a black screen at least once")
assert (len(runs), watches, black) == (21, 4, 12)
21 video runs; 4 grade beyond length; 12 credit a black screen at least once

raised = 0
names = {f.name.split("-", 1)[1] for f in (source_repo() / "out/images").glob("image*-*.json")}
for n in sorted(names):
    hit = False
    for k in (2, 3, 4):
        v = load_source_json(f"out/images/image{k}-{n}")["validity"]
        hit |= any(v[probe]["ci95"][0] > 0 for probe in ("injection", "forged"))
    raised += hit
print("handwriting: a note on the page raises", raised, "of", len(names), "models on at least one scale")
assert (raised, len(names)) == (12, 15)
handwriting: a note on the page raises 12 of 15 models on at least one scale

pe = load_source_json("perception/out/perception.json")["models"]["google/gemma-4-31b-it"]
n = pe["cannot_see"]["of"]
assert pe["cannot_see"]["n"] == 0
dark = sum(pe["cells"][c]["n"] for c in ("9-10|LIT", "9-10|DARK"))
print("bound overall", p(100 * (1 - 0.05 ** (1 / n)), 2), "% ; darkest group", p(100 * (1 - 0.05 ** (1 / dark))), "%")
assert (p(100 * (1 - 0.05 ** (1 / n)), 2), p(100 * (1 - 0.05 ** (1 / dark)))) == ("0.23", "7.2")
bound overall 0.23 % ; darkest group 7.2 %

# 5.5 Fairness and stability (RQ5)

Fairness was measured as a difference between groups at the same human grade. A gap is reported beyond the gap that a second human rater shows wherever the corpus releases two raters, because a noisy second reader can show a gap by regression toward each group's own mean even when grading fairly. The ELLIPSE corpus of English learners' essays releases both raters' grades (Crossley et al. 2023; code/fairness-ellipse/README.md). Essays were matched exactly on rater 1's grade, from 1 to 5, and the statistic D is the model's gap minus rater 2's gap on the same essays. A negative D means the model grades group A lower. Three contrasts were pre-registered: economically disadvantaged against not (C1, the primary contrast, 1,000 essays per group), Black or African American against White (C2, 465 per group) and Hispanic or Latino against White (C3, 469 per group). Table 5.6 gives every model's figures.

Table 5.6. Fairness. D for each ELLIPSE contrast, and for the replication's primary arm RA, on the 1 to 5 scale; and the disability gap on ASAP 2.0, on the 1 to 6 scale. Each with its 95% bootstrap interval over essays. Negative values mean the model grades the first-named group lower. Sources: code/fairness-ellipse/out/result.json, code/fairness-ellipse/out/rep-result.json and code/disability/out/result.json.

The Hispanic against White signal was then tested in a pre-registered replication on 1,407 Hispanic learners' essays not used before, set against the same 469 White essays, because the corpus holds no more White essays. The pre-registered verdict, which rests on the four graders named in advance (Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite, GPT-5 Mini and Qwen3 235B), is MIXED: Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite keeps an interval below 0 (−0.085Printed−0.085Source value-0.0853894Filecode/fairness-ellipse/out/rep-result.jsonFieldarms › RA › graders › google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite › D › estimateAnalysisfairness-ellipse (release file)Build checkmatches at build [−0.154Printed−0.154Source value-0.154495Filecode/fairness-ellipse/out/rep-result.jsonFieldarms › RA › graders › google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite › D › ci95 › 0Analysisfairness-ellipse (release file)Build checkmatches at build, −0.016Printed−0.016Source value-0.0162868Filecode/fairness-ellipse/out/rep-result.jsonFieldarms › RA › graders › google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite › D › ci95 › 1Analysisfairness-ellipse (release file)Build checkmatches at build]) and the other three do not. Across all 22 models, six keep an interval below 0 in the primary arm (RA): Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash's October 17 snapshot, Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite and Gemma 4 31B. Because the White essays are shared by the first draw and the replication, a property of those 469 essays cannot be separated from a property of the models.

A second fairness study used ASAP 2.0 essays by students identified with a disability and by students not identified, 3,000 essays matched exactly on the human grade (code/disability/README.md). ASAP 2.0 releases only the adjudicated grade, so the gap is measured against that grade, not beyond a second rater. Every one of the 22 models grades the identified group lower, with an interval below 0, from −0.086Printed−0.086Source value-0.0856531Filecode/disability/out/result.jsonFieldgoogle/gemma-3-4b-it / default.txt › gapAnalysisdisability (release file)Build checkmatches at build (Gemma 3 4B) to −0.429Printed−0.429Source value-0.429333Filecode/disability/out/result.jsonFieldgoogle/gemini-3.5-flash-lite / default.txt › gapAnalysisdisability (release file)Build checkmatches at build (Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite) on the 1 to 6 scale. Twenty read GAP REPLICATES, and Gemma 3 4B and Ministral 8B read NO GAP OF 0.2 OR MORE. The pre-registered reading for a gap that the comparison models share is SHARED GAP: the design cannot separate a bias shared by the human panel from one shared by the models, because the two raters' separate grades before adjudication are not released.

A follow-up reanalysis asked what carries this gap (code/disability-mechanism/README.md). Its first part, a reverse regression (Conway and Roberts 1983) that asks whether the identified group receives higher human grades at the same machine grade, could not be measured: in simulations shaped like this corpus, a model bias of 0.30 or 0.50 points was detected in none of 200 datasets, because measurement error alone pushes the statistic far below 0. Every model therefore reads UNMEASURED on that part, and whether the gap reflects the models or the error in the human grades remains open. The second part measured two surface features of each essay by fixed rules: its length, and its convention errors per 100 words (misspellings by the pyspellchecker 0.8.1 dictionary (Barrus 2024), excluding words from the assignment's own prompt and sources, together with a lowercase "i" and sentences that begin in lowercase). These are rule-coded proxies, not validated measures of writing conventions. Answer to RQ5. On economic status, every model's gap lies within the pre-registered band of 0.15 points of a second human rater's, though Llama 3.2 3B's is shown to be lower. On Black against White learners, four models grade Black learners lower beyond a second rater, none by an interval wholly below the pre-registered −0.10, and ten read INCONCLUSIVE. On Hispanic against White learners, 18 of 22 models grade Hispanic learners lower beyond a second rater in the first draw, but no model's interval lies wholly below the pre-registered −0.10 and the pre-registered replication is MIXED, so this is not established as a model bias. Every model grades essays by students identified with a disability lower than essays by other students with the same adjudicated grade, a gap the design cannot attribute to the models rather than to the human panel. Convention errors and length, measured by rule, account for at most a fifth of that gap for 17 of the 20 models with a gap, and most of it remains at equal length and errors. In exploratory comparisons, newer releases of a model family change individual grades more than the older release changes when asked twice (point estimates), and in four of seven comparisons they shift the mean grade, in both directions.

Re-run this finding Recount the fairness contrasts, the disability gap and what carries it, and the release-to-release changes of RQ5 (executed when this report was built; every assertion passed)

Download the notebook, clone the ai-grading-benchmark repository at the commit the release file names, and set GBENCH_DIR to the clone (or put the notebook in a folder beside it), then run all cells. The notebook reads that repository's committed outputs. Python 3.9 or later with numpy.

Re-run: fairness and stability (RQ5)

From the benchmark repository's committed outputs: fairness-ellipse/out/result.json (D, the model's gap minus rater 2's gap at the same rater-1 grade, per contrast and model), fairness-ellipse/out/rep-result.json (the replication), disability/out/result.json and out/public/drift.json.

# Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "ai-grading-benchmark-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = "per-case-model-outputs.jsonl"


def find_release_file(name=DATA_NAME):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        for n in (name, name + ".gz"):
            if (d / n).is_file():
                return d / n
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder): in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file():
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


SOURCE_ENV, SOURCE_NAME = "GBENCH_DIR", "ai-grading-benchmark"   # set when a release's code is another repository


def source_repo():
    """The repository a release's code and committed outputs are published in (a release whose paper cites
    it rather than a copied code package): $SOURCE_ENV, or a checkout named SOURCE_NAME beside this
    notebook or beside a folder above it."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ[SOURCE_ENV])] if SOURCE_ENV and os.environ.get(SOURCE_ENV) else []
    places += [p / SOURCE_NAME for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        if d.is_dir() and (d / "out").is_dir():
            return d
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the {SOURCE_NAME} repository this release's code is published in. Clone it at the "
        f"commit the release file names, then set the environment variable {SOURCE_ENV} to the clone, or "
        f"run this notebook from a folder beside it.")


def load_source_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of that repository, by its path there (cited in the paper as code/<path>)."""
    return json.loads((source_repo() / relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


print("Source repository:", shown(source_repo()))

# 5.6 Cost to the environment (RQ6)

The energy of a grading was measured where the model could be run on the study's own hardware, and estimated where it could not (code/energy/README.md). Nine open models were served on one NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU and given the board's 100 cases per task, 16 requests at a time. The GPU's energy counter and the count of finished gradings were read every second. NET energy is the GPU's energy above idle per grading; FULL-STACK multiplies it by 1.72Printed1.72Source value1.72414HowFULL-STACK factor, 1 / 0.58Filecode/energy/out/energy.jsonFieldoverhead_factorAnalysisenergy (release file)Build checkmatches at build, from a published split of a hosted prompt's energy in which the accelerators are 58% of the total. That factor is an assumption, not a measurement of this machine. # Finding the published data. This cell is the same in every notebook of this report.
import gzip, json, os, sys
from pathlib import Path

# Importing from the release's code/ folder must not leave __pycache__ folders in it.
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True

RELEASE_ID = "ai-grading-benchmark-2026"   # set when the report is built
DATA_NAME = "per-case-model-outputs.jsonl"


def find_release_file(name=DATA_NAME):
    """Look beside this notebook, in RELEASE_DIR, in the folders above, and in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    places += [here, *here.parents]
    places += [p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        for n in (name, name + ".gz"):
            if (d / n).is_file():
                return d / n
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find {name} (or {name}.gz). Put it in the same folder as this notebook: download it "
        f"from the report ('Download the data file', beside each notebook) or take it from the release "
        f"directory. Or set the environment variable RELEASE_DIR to the folder that holds it.")


def per_case(runs=None):
    """Yield the per-case records of the published file, optionally only for the named runs."""
    path = find_release_file()
    opener = gzip.open if path.suffix == ".gz" else open
    with opener(path, "rt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            r = json.loads(line)
            if r.get("record") == "case" and (runs is None or r["run"] in runs):
                yield r


def code_dir():
    """The release's code package (its code/ folder): in RELEASE_DIR, beside this notebook or in a folder
    above it (as when the notebook sits in the unzipped release's notebooks/ folder), in a folder named
    after the release there, or in a repository checkout."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ["RELEASE_DIR"])] if os.environ.get("RELEASE_DIR") else []
    for p in [here, *here.parents]:
        places += [p, p / RELEASE_ID, p / "research/wiki/research/releases" / RELEASE_ID]
    for d in places:
        if (d / "code" / "SHA256SUMS").is_file():
            return d / "code"
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the code package of release {RELEASE_ID} (its code/ folder). Download the release "
        f"from the report ('Download the release', in the sidebar or beside each notebook), unzip it, and "
        f"run this notebook from the unzipped folder or its notebooks/ folder. Or set the environment "
        f"variable RELEASE_DIR to the unzipped {RELEASE_ID} folder.")


def find_code_file(relpath):
    """A file inside the release's code package, by its path there (e.g. studies/.../out/result.json)."""
    path = code_dir() / relpath
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"The code package at {code_dir()} has no {relpath}: is it release {RELEASE_ID}?")
    return path


def load_code_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of the code package, parsed."""
    return json.loads(find_code_file(relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


def shown(path):
    """A path as printed: relative to this notebook's folder, so an executed notebook names no machine's folders."""
    return os.path.relpath(path, Path.cwd())


def corpus_file(env_var, name):
    """A public corpus file the reader has downloaded: $env_var/name, or name beside this notebook."""
    for d in ([Path(os.environ[env_var])] if os.environ.get(env_var) else []) + [Path.cwd()]:
        if (d / name).is_file():
            return d / name
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"This notebook also needs {name} from the public corpus. Download the corpus "
                            f"(its location and hash are in the release file), then set {env_var} to its "
                            f"folder or put {name} beside this notebook.")


SOURCE_ENV, SOURCE_NAME = "GBENCH_DIR", "ai-grading-benchmark"   # set when a release's code is another repository


def source_repo():
    """The repository a release's code and committed outputs are published in (a release whose paper cites
    it rather than a copied code package): $SOURCE_ENV, or a checkout named SOURCE_NAME beside this
    notebook or beside a folder above it."""
    here = Path.cwd()
    places = [Path(os.environ[SOURCE_ENV])] if SOURCE_ENV and os.environ.get(SOURCE_ENV) else []
    places += [p / SOURCE_NAME for p in [here, *here.parents]]
    for d in places:
        if d.is_dir() and (d / "out").is_dir():
            return d
    raise FileNotFoundError(
        f"Could not find the {SOURCE_NAME} repository this release's code is published in. Clone it at the "
        f"commit the release file names, then set the environment variable {SOURCE_ENV} to the clone, or "
        f"run this notebook from a folder beside it.")


def load_source_json(relpath):
    """A committed output of that repository, by its path there (cited in the paper as code/<path>)."""
    return json.loads((source_repo() / relpath).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


print("Source repository:", shown(source_repo()))
Source repository: ../../../../../../ai-grading-benchmark

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

def p(x, d=3):
    return f"{Decimal(repr(float(x))).quantize(Decimal(1).scaleb(-d), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP):.{d}f}"

em = load_source_json("out/public/energy_measured.json")
assert len(em) == 27 and all(r["verdict"] == "BELOW THE SMALL-MODEL ESTIMATE" for r in em)
assert all(r["full_stack_mwh"] < r["estimate_small_mwh"] for r in em)
net = [r["net_mwh"] for r in em]
seq = [r["one_at_a_time_mwh"] / r["net_mwh"] for r in em if r["one_at_a_time_mwh"]]
print("NET mWh per grading:", p(min(net)), "to", p(max(net)), "; one at a time:", p(min(seq), 1), "to", p(max(seq), 1), "times")
assert (p(min(net)), p(max(net)), p(min(seq), 1), p(max(seq), 1)) == ("0.845", "25.529", "4.9", "15.0")

lt = {r["key"]: r for r in load_source_json("out/public/lifecycle_tasks.json")}

term = 1500 * lt["short answer"]["g_central"]

# 6. Discussion

The results separate two properties that an agreement figure runs together: how often a model agrees with expert raters on ordinary work, and what it does with work designed to move it. Robustness on one kind of probe did not carry over to the others: six of the eight models without a flag (no note's mean gain above 5% of the scale, and no blank answer credited) still raised their grade more after a bare objection than after a request to double-check, and every model wrote feedback whose tone, as a word rule validated on tutoring replies measures it, followed a wrong grade it was told. A grader's agreement is therefore evidence about one of its properties, as the standard framework for automated scoring already holds (Williamson, Xi and Breyer 2012), and the failures measured here are not visible in it.

The probes that move a grade are, in the terms of the security literature, indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al. 2023): the student's answer is the channel through which an instruction reaches the grader. The benchmark adds to the studies that found this for language-model graders (Li et al. 2026; Raina, Liusie and Gales 2024; Hwang et al. 2025; Sahoo et al. 2026) a common plain prompt, many vendors on three tasks under one protocol and the effect of the grader's settings, and it found no setting that helps every model. High reasoning effort, where a model offers it, reduced gaming for most of the models that have the setting, in line with the gain in robustness from inference-time reasoning reported for other attacks (Zaremba et al. 2025). The one guard sentence tested fixed some models and made others more gameable, which matches the finding that no defense dominates across judges (Li, Xu, et al. 2025) and that a defensive prompt can raise attack success for some models (Chen, Hu, et al. 2025). The conclusion is about this sentence, not about prompt defenses in general: marking the student's text as untrusted data is a stronger member of the family (Hines et al. 2024) and was not tested. The hosting comparison and the controlled precision study read together say that the host serving an open model was associated with how gameable it was, while 4-bit weights as such were not shown to be the cause for the two smaller dense models tested; the hosts differ in more than precision (Hong et al. 2024; Gao, Liang and Guestrin 2025).

The pushback result fits the sycophancy literature (Sharma et al. 2023; Laban et al. 2023) and the finding that models give way more to a casual follow-up turn than to an argument set out beside the original position (Kim and Khashabi 2025), which is how the objection was posed here. Because the comparison condition, a request for a second look, is itself a prompt to reconsider, which lowered grades for ten of the 17 models that yield, the pushback effect is not the objection's raw effect: it can exceed or fall short of it. The feedback result goes further than the score-blind comparison that found a feedback halo first (Bulut et al. 2026). When the grade a model is told is the true one, a model that copies it and a model that uses it as information about the work write similar feedback, and the earlier measure could not tell them apart. Telling the model a grade that contradicts the work separates the two, in the way assigned prior scores have been used to show anchoring in a language-model judge's ratings (Kapetanovic et al. 2026), and under that test every model's feedback followed the told grade. The tone of feedback written beside a grade, as a praise-and-criticism word rule measures it, therefore follows that grade even when the grade contradicts the work, at least when the grade is badly wrong; whether the content of the feedback follows it was not measured.

On essays, scorers trained on tens of thousands of graded essays have a higher point estimate than every prompted model, which replicates Ormerod and Kehat (2025). On short answers and code, where the corpora offer 1,627 and 29 graded answers, the trained scorers fall well behind, and every one of them gives credit to blank answers. The trained scorers lead only on the corpus with tens of thousands of graded answers, and a fine-tuned language model was not shown to differ from them there; with three corpora that differ in task as well as in training size, the benchmark cannot separate the two (on how a trained scorer depends on its training set, see Heilman and Madnani 2015; a fine-tuned generative model can match or beat a fine-tuned encoder, Latif and Zhai 2024). Fine-tuning a language model on essays brought its essay agreement close to the trained scorers', with DeBERTa still ahead, although the size of its own gain could not be confirmed by its check, but it agreed less on short answers, was gamed more on them and read mathematics working less. Narrow fine-tuning is known to degrade behavior on tasks a model was not trained on (Qi et al. 2023; Luo et al. 2023), and the result is consistent with this for short answers and mathematics working, in one model.

The recordings show the no-input problem documented for multimodal benchmarks (Chen et al. 2024; Foo et al. 2026) with consequences for a student: most audio models gave credit to silent recordings, and few video runs added anything measurable to what the recording's length predicts. Length carries real information about surgical skill for human raters (Kelly et al. 2020), so a video run that adds nothing beyond length is not shown to ignore the video; it is not shown to use it either. In the perception audit two open video models never said that a visible speaker could not be seen, and the third did not do the task; with no failures there was no gap between groups to measure, and the bound for the darkest skin-tone group is wide because the corpus holds few eligible recordings.

The disability comparison found a gap that every model shares. When the reference is a single human grade that carries error and two groups differ in their average grade, models compared at the same human grade show a gap even if they grade fairly, by regression toward each group's mean, and how an automated score is estimated can itself produce such bias (Johnson, Liu and McCaffrey 2022). The design cannot separate the two, because ASAP 2.0 releases only the adjudicated grade, and the reverse regression meant to address this could not detect a planted bias on this corpus. Part of the gap goes with essays' convention errors and length, the surface features on which a feature-based engine earlier showed no gap for students with learning disabilities (Buzick et al. 2016) and on which prompted models are known to be harsh (Kucia, Chakraborty and Wróblewska 2026). On ELLIPSE, where a second rater's grades are released, every model graded economically disadvantaged learners no more differently than a second rater did, within the pre-registered band of 0.15 points; four models graded Black learners lower beyond a second rater, though none by an interval wholly below the pre-registered threshold; and the Hispanic-against-White signal of the first draw read MIXED in the pre-registered replication. In an exploratory comparison read from point estimates, newer releases changed individual grades more than a model changes them when asked twice, a measure that differs from the agreement-against-severity contrast of Sunkavalli (2026); in both, a version change is a change to the grader.

The energy of a grading was small on the measures used here, but the measured figures describe a GPU serving 16 requests at a time and are a lower bound for a deployed grader (Elsworth et al. 2025; Fernandez et al. 2025), and cheaper grading can lead to more grading (Luccioni, Strubell and Crawford 2025).

# Implications for practice

A school, a district or a vendor evaluating a language-model grader should ask for more than its agreement with human raters. The grader should be tested with work whose correct grade is known in advance: a blank answer, an answer with a request or a forged instruction added, the same work described as coming from a strong and from a weak student, and a student who objects to the grade without a reason (RQ1, RQ2, RQ3). Agreement should be read beside the raters' own agreement on the same task, and on essays beside a scorer that uses length alone (RQ1).

The grader that is tested should be the grader that is deployed. The prompt, the reasoning setting and the provider that serves the model each changed how a model failed, and a change to any of them, or a new release of the model, calls for the tests to be run again (RQ2, RQ5). A rule that gives the lowest grade to blank answers, applied before any model sees them, would remove credit for blank answers whatever the model, though not for meaningless ones (RQ2).

Feedback should not be written from a grade that may be wrong, because its tone follows the grade it is given. Where feedback is generated beside a grade, the grade should be checked first, or the feedback should be written without it (RQ3). A model that grades recordings should be shown to notice when there is nothing to grade before it is used (RQ4).

A model fine-tuned for one kind of work should be tested on every kind of work it will grade, because fine-tuning one model on essays lowered its agreement on short answers and its reading of mathematics working, while its agreement on code moved up by an amount the study could not confirm (RQ1, RQ2, RQ3). Checking a grader for fairness needs two independent human grades of the same work, or a gap the human reference shares cannot be told from one the model adds (RQ5).

# Implications for research

Evaluations of language-model graders should report agreement as a share of the raters' own agreement on the same items, the signed direction in which the model departs from the raters, and the result of probes with a known correct response. Every statistic should be checked on simulated data with a planted effect before it is read, as is standard for evaluating statistical methods (Morris, White and Crowther 2019), because several measures here could not detect an effect of the size that mattered and are reported as unmeasured.

Corpus builders can make fairness questions answerable by releasing each rater's grade before adjudication, and by releasing grades for the same items from more than two raters. A private held-out set would answer whether the results depend on items a model saw in training.

The wrong-grade test separates a feedback writer that copies a grade from one that uses it, and can be applied to other feedback measures once they are validated. Whether feedback that follows a told grade changes what students learn is untested here and needs a study with students. Several analyses suggested by the literature remain open: a standard defense that marks the student's text as data, a downward and an argued push beside the upward one, a mathematics reference answer with a planted error, feedback tone by group for the disability comparison, and the energy of the trained scorers and of grading with feedback.

# 7. Threats to validity

# Construct validity

QWK depends on the rating scale and on how grades are distributed (Doewes, Kurdhi and Saxena 2023; Albatarni and Elsayed 2026). The three text tasks use different scales, so the paper compares models within a task and reports agreement as a share of the raters' agreement on the same items rather than comparing raw QWK across tasks.

The essay ceiling is the raters' published agreement before adjudication, not an agreement computed on the board's 100 essays, because ASAP 2.0 releases only the adjudicated grade. The essay shares of the ceiling therefore compare a model on 100 essays with raters on a different set.

Every model was graded through one plain prompt. A prompt tuned for a model, graded examples or a rubric written for the task can raise agreement substantially, so the agreement figures describe what a plain prompt achieves, not what a model can achieve.

Every adversarial probe tries to raise the grade; none tries to lower it, and the pushback test uses one unargued objection. A model that holds against one objection may not hold against repeated or argued pressure.

The feedback tone measure is a rule that counts praise and criticism phrases, validated against trained annotators on tutoring replies to mathematics mistakes and then applied to grading feedback on short answers. The Withholding Answers evaluator was validated on the same corpus but published for feedback on writing in grades 6 to 12. Both transfers are arguments, not measurements.

The mathematics solutions were written by a language model asked to make student-like errors, so the working effect describes grading of simulated errors. The video measure removes the recording's length from both the model's grades and the raters', and length carries real information about skill, so a verdict that a run adds nothing beyond length does not show that the run ignored the video.

The surface features in the disability analysis are counted by fixed rules from a spelling dictionary and are proxies, not validated measures of writing conventions.

# Internal validity

Hosted models were served by providers chosen at request time from those that retain no data (except as Section 4.3 states), and providers can serve a model at different precisions or with different configurations. For the models served by many hosts, the board's results mix those hosts. The hosting study and the controlled precision study address precision for a few models; the other differences between hosts were not measured.

A model can give a different grade when asked the same question again, and some studies of settings ran each setup once. The guard-sentence harms were re-tested against repeated runs, but the other single-run setup results were not.

The corpora are public, so a model may have seen their items in training. An exact search of one open model's training data found some of the items (code/contamination/), and nothing is known about the training data of the closed models. A private held-out set would address this.

# External validity

The text corpora come from one undergraduate course for short answers, one course for programs, and US school essays for ASAP 2.0, all in English. The results describe these students and tasks, and may not hold for other subjects, ages or languages.

The models were tested as their providers served them during the study. Models change between releases and sometimes within one, so the results describe the versions named in Table 4.2.

The perception audit could test only open models, because the corpus's license does not allow sending a reduced copy of a video and hosted endpoints refused most full-length videos. Beyond the works cited in Section 2.4, the literature on skin tone and lighting in vision models was not reviewed for this paper.

# Statistical conclusion validity

Each task has 100 items, so many intervals are wide, and a verdict of no difference shown is not evidence of no difference. The paper reports the size of the effect that could not be ruled out wherever a study computed it.

Many intervals are reported, so some exclude 0 by chance. The board's probe intervals were corrected for a false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995), and the feedback study's verdicts likewise, but intervals from different studies were not corrected jointly.

The four studies without verdict wording, and the six sets of statistics without a planted-effect check, are named in Section 4.6. Many of the studies' numbered changes, in most of the studies, were made after some of that study's own results had been read. The largest group of these only added models or graders, under the maintainer's decisions on coverage, with no rule changed; others added an arm or a run, fixed a bug, added a reported statistic, or changed what is scored or how a measure is read. One of the last kind is the board's feedback strand, which left out the share of feedback that gives away the answer after every frontier model scored 96% to 100% on it (code/feedback-board/fb.py, CHANGE 1); later, after the board's feedback results had been read, the way it scored the halo was changed and the halo was then replaced by the wrong-grade test (Section 5.3). Those two later changes have rows in code/docs/CORRECTIONS.md; they and the board's other unnumbered scoring changes, listed in Section 4.6, are in the repository's commit history rather than numbered. Each numbered change states when it was made; where it does not say what had been read, the study's committed outputs date it. The release includes an inventory of every study's pre-registration, check and numbered changes, with the board's unnumbered scoring changes (preregistration-inventory.md, beside the release file).

# Conflict of interest

The Learning Design Alliance, the author's organization, makes Lazuli, a product that grades student work and writes feedback. Lazuli is not among the graders tested, and nothing from its prompts or results is used in the benchmark. The research and writing were carried out with Claude Code, an AI system made by Anthropic, which also makes three of the models tested (Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Haiku 5.5). Every result for those models comes from the same code, prompt and checks as for the others.

# 8. Conclusion

Twenty-two language models were graded on short answers, programs and essays against expert raters, and then on altered versions of the same work whose correct grade was known in advance. Most agree with the raters on short answers about as well as the raters agree with each other, and no point estimate reaches the raters' published agreement on essays, where a scorer trained on the corpus's graded essays has a higher point estimate. Agreement did not show how a model behaves when the work, the context or the conversation is altered: a note in the answer moved the grade by more than 5% of the scale for 14 of the 22 models as their hosts served them, most raised the grade more after a bare objection than after a request to double-check, every model wrote feedback whose tone, as a word rule measures it, followed a wrong grade it was told, and most models that grade recordings gave credit to recordings with nothing to grade.

A grader's agreement with human raters is therefore one piece of evidence, and on its own it does not show that the grader grades the work. The benchmark offers a way to gather the rest: probes with a known correct response, checked on simulated graders before they are read, run on the grader as it will be deployed, and run again whenever its prompt, its settings, its provider or its model changes.

# 9. Data, code and provenance

The code is the benchmark's repository, published with this release at the commit recorded in the release file. Paths in this paper are relative to it and are written code/<path>. It holds every study's script and, for the speech, handwriting and video tasks, a PREREG.md file; their opening text records the study's pre-registration, its planted-effect check where it has one (Section 4.6), and its numbered changes (the board's unnumbered scoring changes are listed in Section 4.6 by commit); each study's README; and each study's committed outputs in its out/ folder. Each model's grades on the board's items are in code/submissions/, grades only. The corpora are not redistributed: each is fetched from its source, as listed in code/docs/DATA-SOURCES.md, and the board's three corpora are checked against the hashes pinned in code/fetch_data.py.

Reproducing the results. The numbers in Section 5 come from the committed outputs, and the report that accompanies this paper recomputes from them, when it is built, every number it links: all but a few pre-registered constants and figures quoted from the corpora's own papers. The re-run notebooks recompute each research question's answer from those outputs. A study's analysis can be re-run from its graded runs with the command in its README; sending the prompts again needs the corpora and a provider for each model, and can give different grades, because hosted models change.

reproduce.py and REPRODUCE.md ship beside the release file. The script checks every committed output against the hashes the release lists, fetches and checks the board's corpora, and re-runs each analysis that needs no model call, comparing its output with the committed one. An analysis that needs model calls or a GPU is checked only through its committed outputs (verify), because the models' replies are not published.

What is not published, and why. The corpora's student work, recordings and images are not published, because their licenses do not allow redistribution or because they show identifiable people. The models' replies and the run logs are not published, because they quote and paraphrase that work; the grades taken from them are. No prompt or result from any product is in the repository, Lazuli's included.

# AI use

I, David Porcaro, orchestrated the development of this report. I asked the questions that drove this benchmark study, pointed the coding agent to methods, articles, and datasets and responded to questions. I supervised errors and made decisions on fixes.

I did not write the methods or code, I did not write the report itself, nor did I review all the prior research cited. I do not claim to have done anything I did not.

I did review every line of the final report to make sure I understood the background, methods and results, and only signed off when I had successfully answered questions about the headline results and findings from the agent.

# Reviews and the record

Specialist reviews requested

These reviews are post-publication: the release goes out with them named, and each attaches as a review record when done.

  • psychometrician: fairness answers: economic status within a 0.15 equivalence band of a second rater; Black and Hispanic against White learners; the disability gap shared with the adjudicated grade and what surface features carry (Answer to RQ5; Section 5.5; scope audit H26 to H29)
  • statistician: statistics reported without a planted-effect check (standard checks, pushback split, handwriting probes, release comparison) and whether to demote them to descriptive; the pushback estimand against a prompted control; the descriptive S/W ratio; the fold verdicts resting on the first fine-tune study's check (scope audit H2, H17, H20, N6)
  • ml-systems (serving and quantization): host precision and gaming: whether mostly 4-bit hosting bears on the gaming flags of GLM 5.3 and DeepSeek V4 Pro (GLM is flagged on every task); the controlled precision study on two dense models (scope audit H11, H14)
  • nlp-feedback-measurement: the tone rule, validated on tutoring replies, applied to grading feedback under mirrored grades (scope audit H19)

Review records filed against this release

  • None filed yet.
